info.bio:
Gary Numan (nacido Gary Anthony James Webb el 8 de marzo de 1958) es un cantante y compositor británico, pionero del electropop.

La carrera musical de Gary Numan empieza a mediados de la década de los 70 cuando, después de abandonar su posición como guitarrista de Laser, una la banda londinense de punk, forma junto con el bajista Paul Gardiner su propio grupo: Tubeway Army. Después de grabar un primer álbum de maquetas más próximo al punk

scenes.name: Funk industrial
scenes.book: Funk: The Music, the People, and the Rhythm of the One
scenes.author: Rickey Vincent
scenes.desc: Tras la caída de P-Funk, muchos ritmos nuevos vinieron de fuera: Kraftwerk, Art of Noise («Beat Box», «Close (to the Edit)»), Talking Heads (Stop Making Sense, con Bernie Worrell) y el «Genius of Love» de Tom Tom Club. Herbie Hancock pidió a su mánager Tony Meilandt unos temas de hip hop y con Bill Laswell y Grandmixer D.S.T. hizo «Rockit» (Future Shock, 1983): la cima del funk industrial nada más empezar. Laswell (Material, Time Zone con John Lydon, Manu Dibango, los Last Poets) dejó su sello de bajo grueso; sellos como Celluloid, On-U Sound, Tommy Boy o Def Jam sacaban ritmos ásperos de raspados metálicos y tensión de Guerra Fría. On-U Sound de Adrian Sherwood fichó a la sección rítmica de Sugarhill (Doug Wimbish, Skip McDonald, Keith LeBlanc): Tackhead, el «No Sell Out» con la voz de Malcolm X, «el P-Funk de los ochenta» según Pedro Bell.
scenes.family: Hip hop, go-go y funk de los noventa

scenes.name: Ultravox, John Foxx y Gary Numan
scenes.book: Postpunk. Romper todo y empezar de nuevo
scenes.author: Simon Reynolds
scenes.desc: El primer synthpop de masas. Ultravox, glam tardío para la crítica, se vuelve europeo con John Foxx y el productor Conny Plank (Systems of Romance, 1978: «I Want to Be a Machine», «My Sex», «Hiroshima Mon Amour»); Foxx sigue solo con Metamatic, todo sintetizadores. Gary Numan encuentra por casualidad un mini-Moog en el estudio Spaceward y convierte canciones punk en electrónicas: «Are 'Friends' Electric?» de Tubeway Army (1979) llega al número uno y abre los rankings a los sintetizadores. Hard rock con pátina futurista, espectáculo glam, una saga de ciencia ficción sobre una megacomputadora y una vulnerabilidad sexual ambigua que conquista a los adolescentes: «versiones caricaturescas» de Unknown Pleasures y Closer.

scenes.name: Synth-pop y new romantics
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Todo empieza con los instrumentos electrónicos, el futurismo melódico de Eno y los ritmos robóticos de Kraftwerk: el synth-pop es quizá el acontecimiento más importante de la música melódica desde el Mersey-beat. The Buggles («Video Killed The Radio Star»), Gary Numan, Yellow Magic Orchestra, OMD, Depeche Mode, Human League; con Soft Cell llega el diluvio y el dúo de teclista y cantante se impone (Eurythmics, Yazoo, Erasure, Pet Shop Boys). Flying Lizards y New Order («Blue Monday»). Los nuevos ídolos adolescentes, los new romantics: Duran Duran, Culture Club, Thompson Twins, Tears For Fears, ABC, Heaven 17.

scenes.name: Electro-funk
scenes.book: Loops 1 y 2. Una historia de la música electrónica
scenes.author: Javier Blánquez (ed.)
scenes.desc: El primer hip hop descubre los ritmos robóticos de Kraftwerk: fantasía futurista y poshumana con voces metálicas, ritmos rotos y bajos del diámetro de Saturno.

podcast.title: Times Square Soundtrack Contribution (1980)
podcast.body: Gary Numan contributed to the soundtrack for the 1980 movie *Time Square*. This soundtrack gained recognition for being one of the pioneering compilations to feature the emerging alternative music of the day, including punk rock and new wave. "The soundtrack featured the pretenders, Roxy music, Gary Newman, XTC, Joe Jackson."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
srcs.episode: Key Alt-Rock Movie Soundtracks

podcast.title: Accomplished Pilot and Stunt Flying (1981)
podcast.body: Gary Numan, a new wave star who transitioned into an electronic music icon and influenced artists like Beck and Dave Grohl, became a highly accomplished pilot. He even worked as a stunt pilot in air shows. However, he ceased stunt flying after four members of his six-person flying team, plus his instructor, were killed in separate accidents. In 1981, he successfully flew around the world in his own aircraft. "Gary Newman, the new wave star, turned electronic icon to guys like Back in Dave Grohl, became very accomplished as a pilot, even working as a stunt pilot in air shows."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music

podcast.title: Alien-like Image
podcast.body: Gary Numan cultivated a sharp visual image, described as resembling a "cold, detached alien" and likened to "Ziggy Stardust's love child." This look, characterized by sharp suits, ties, and perfectly groomed hair, was part of a broader aesthetic linked to the dehumanized electronic music sound that emerged in the late 1970s. "Meanwhile Gary Newman looked sharp too, but also a lot like some kind of cold detached alien. Maybe it was Ziggy Stardust's love child."

podcast.title: Aviation Aspirations and Stunt Pilot Career
podcast.body: Gary Numan initially aspired to be a professional pilot, but his music career took precedence. Despite this, he has achieved professional status as both a stunt and test pilot, engaging in aerobatics, flight formations, and flying vintage World War II planes. He temporarily gave up flying due to losing friends in accidents and crashes. "He's now both a stunt and test pilot, aerobatics, flight formations, flying vintage World War II planes."

podcast.title: Mini-Moog Inspiring Genre Shift
podcast.body: An unattended Mini-Moog left in a studio had a profound impact on Gary Numan, inspiring him to completely abandon playing guitars. This pivotal moment led to his creation of influential new wave technopop hits. "A Mini-Mog left unattended in a studio, inspired Gary Newman to give up on guitars completely, resulting in new wave technopop hits like Cars and our friends electric."

podcast.title: Robotic and Dystopian Aesthetic
podcast.body: Gary Numan's "Are 'Friends' Electric?" showcased a vibe that was robotic, cold, deliberately artificial, emotionally sterile, and intense, mirroring the dystopian and alienated lyrical themes of early Technopop. This particular aesthetic was a slight variation of the nihilism found in guitar-driven punk. "And note the vibe of that song. Much of early technopop was robotic, cold, deliberately artificial, emotionally sterile, and just generally a little intense."

podcast.title: Synthesizer Discovery and Creative Shift
podcast.body: In the spring of 1979, Gary Numan, who had previously favored guitars, encountered a Mini-Moog synthesizer in a studio. This spontaneous discovery radically altered his musical direction, leading him to abandon plans for a punk album and instead explore the concept of electronic punk songs, marking a pivotal moment in his career and the development of Technopop. "Another milestone in the creation of Tectopop came in the spring of 1979, when Gary Newman, previously a big fan of guitars, started playing with the new synthesizer someone had left in a studio, was a mini-mog."

xref.title: Nash the Slash (Jeff Plunman, Toronto, 1948–2014) – Surgical Bandages Adopted After Three Mile Island Accident (1979); David Gilmour Offered Guitar Part but Nash Refused All Guitars
xref.body: Nash the Slash's real name was Jeff Plunman, born in Toronto on March 26, 1948. The stage name came from a character in a 1927 Laurel and Hardy silent film. He co-founded the prog band FM in 1975 and audiences could see his face briefly, but after the nuclear accident at Three Mile Island near Harrisburg, Pennsylvania in March 1979, Nash adopted surgical bandages that completely obscured his face as a way of raising awareness about what could happen if a nuclear plant melted down. He left FM around 1980 to resume his solo career, toured with Gary Numan and the Tubes, hung out with Iggy Pop and Daniel Lanois, and Brian Eno collaborated on his records. David Gilmour of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs — but Nash refused because he never used guitars on any of his songs. He made records until 2012, was especially popular in Germany and Poland, and died of an apparent heart attack at his Toronto home on May 10, 2014, at age 66. His music and costumes are managed by the Nash the Slash Legacy organization and much was donated to the National Music Center in Calgary. His best-known record was 1984's American Bandages. "David Gilmore of Pink Floyd was such a fan that he offered to lay down a guitar part on one of Nash's songs, but Nash refused because he never, ever used guitars on any of his songs."

xref.title: Feminization of Male Rock Stars
xref.body: Bowie was the first to openly and unabashedly feminize the macho male rock and roll star. His pioneering embrace of androgyny led to a subsequent wave of acts that were androgynous, bisexual, gay, or "plain femme looking," including artists like Depeche Mode, Gary Numan, Soft Cell, and Eurythmics. "Bowie was the first to unabashedly and openly feminize the macho male rock and roll star."
